title: Caller and Wiggs on how jazz originated: field hands, minstrels, slaves and minuets
summary: A caller credits work songs and minstrel parades; Wiggs gives his version of slaves imitating the madam's minuets and the African scale behind the blues.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Good morning, Joe. Mr. Wiggs, I enjoyed that last record of yours. I thought it was mighty fine. Thank you. How old are you, sir? I'm only 70. Only 70? I'm a stripling. Uh-huh. Well, Joe claims I'm over 100, so I... Oh, get away now. Outdate you. Not with that voice. Not with that voice. You're not anywhere near. Anyway, I've never heard anybody explain how jazz originally originated. And as a boy, well, I say that jazz first started for music songs that were sung by the field hands. I used to listen to them. Convict labor gangs, railroad section hands, and dock wallopers. They would make up their songs as they would go along. Do you remember that, Mr. Wiggs? Yeah. And they were mostly blues numbers and such famous blues numbers as Frankie and Johnny, the Wabash Blues, Memphis Blues, St. Louis Blues, Bill Street Blues, etc. I believe were all derived from that. And also, when I was a boy, do you remember these traveling minstrel shows? Oh, yeah. You know, they used to go around and play in Longtown. Oh, do I remember them, yeah. Yeah. Bunk Johnson played in one of those. And I remember one that was named Silas Green from New Orleans. Yeah, yeah, I remember that. He was no relative of mine. But anyway, they would hold a parade down the street, you know, prior to their show. And they would play these blues numbers and they'd say, man, let's jazz it up. And they would. And I say that's where jazz originally came from. And most of the stuff I hear around New Orleans has no relationship to that whatsoever, whereas yours that I just listened to did. Well, now, let me give you my version of it. Of course, I can't document. No one can document the beginning of jazz. But this is my version of it. I'm going back to the slave era now. And, of course, the slaves were very poor. And they heard the madam playing these minuets in the living room. And these poor guys would sometimes make an instrument for themselves. And sometimes they'd be lucky enough to pull an old battered-up clarinet or cornette out of a garbage can, you know. And they began to play what they thought was the tune that the madam played. Now, she may have been playing this minuet from which Tiger Rag came. Or she may have been playing something else. But anyway, that's where Tiger Rag came from. Was it a French minuet or an English minuet, Dick? Good stuff. Thank you.
Well, it's supposed to have been from a French quadrille, originally, that is one story.

French quadrille. I don't know how to say that big word anyway. But to me, that's the way jazz was born. There was no particular time that it was born. It was just born from these poor people with this enormous amount of gift that the black person has in almost any subject you want to mention. And that was his treatment. They still do it nowadays. You can hear some of these old-timers. Instead of playing an F sharp, they'll play an F natural, you know, and their ear won't hear. They've been doing it for 50 years, you know, making the same mistake for 50 years. And they go right on, and, of course, people overlook that because the rest of the stuff has got so much life in it and so much attack and vim. And that's what their ear hears, you see. And it's different from the white music because of the scale which they used in Africa. And the scale, of course, is still in the black person's ear from Africa. And that's one reason why you get that blues sound, because they bend the note to try to get it up or down to the European scale, the scale that America uses in their music. Well, I'll stick by the old-time blues. The type of jazz they play today to me is just a lot of racket.
